writing.note: Seven distinct specimens verified. Modern Bambara, Yeke and Bagirmi examples are explicitly modern; Kazembe is a Portuguese external publication; Njube is English; Fula is an undated manuscript in scholarly Latin transcription; Omar is a dated Arabic autobiographical witness. No fabricated historic script or translation identified.

sourceBudget.method: Whitespace words; overview, any override summary counted independently, every period summary, section item and ending charged fully to each attributed source. No deduplication of repeated summary text.

checkedSources.detail: Primary text directly checked for royal appearance, Manchester cloth, queen, reed enclosure, gardens, and 1 January 1868 iron hoes exchanged for calico. Concrete details supported.
Indexed African Studies Centre curated abstract confirms Kazembe defeat in 1899 followed by negotiated colonial chiefship. Its erroneous Msiri date is not used in this draft.

Indexed UFSC catalogue confirms the Portuguese Gamito title and 1937 edition. Direct catalogue URL returned 404; UFSC literature catalogue and Smithsonian catalogue also confirm title. Correctly labeled an outsider publication, not local royal writing.
Direct AfricaMuseum narrative confirms arrival of Stairs in December 1891, Msiri death on 20 December, flag on 30 December, and subsequent colonial collaboration.

Indexed royal heritage song page confirms Linumba and French heading La Grande Maison. Modern printed title explicitly differentiated from nineteenth-century writing; combined original/translation below ten lyric words.
Direct Met exhibition narrative confirms Biton, military association and 1861 conquest by Umar Tal.

Direct Chapter XV confirms four towns, flat roofs, whitewash, ferry fare, enslaved operators, joined tree trunks, horses, household fish/mat/lamp, cotton spinning. Two corrections accepted: Park recorded fare but was forbidden passage; hospitable woman is unnamed.
Peace Corps PDF page 5, Lesson 3 directly confirms exact Bambara greeting and English translation. Modern Latin orthography clearly labeled.
Direct TDV historical entry supports court conversion, regional dependencies and forced French protection, followed by changing treaty arrangements. No single simple disappearance asserted.
Direct Annie Lebeuf 1967 account supports old capital remains, brick palace/mosque and 1898 abandonment/burning during conflict with Rabih.
Direct primary travel text confirms rice pudding/dates at Sambore, reciprocal coffee hospitality, and language name tar Bagrimma with source accents. These are attributed traveller encounters.
Direct CLBA publisher page confirms Kup an Duniya and English title, Genesis subject, named translator, and Roman/Arabic script formats. Correctly identified as modern publication.
Direct Zimbabwe museum page supports Mzilikazi migration, multiethnic state, Old Bulawayo 1870, relocation 1881, reconstruction and later fire.
Direct University of Edinburgh transcription section 16 confirms 14 October 1898 letter and exact home-for-holiday sentence, including fore. English language and exile provenance correctly signaled.
Direct scholarly article section 3.2 supports BSAC conquest in 1893 and distinguishes colonial justifications from history.
Direct TDV entry supports Poredaka defeat and end of independent rule in 1896.
Direct BU manuscript catalogue confirms Fula Ajami, handwritten unpublished manuscript, Conakry provenance, and no historical date supplied. Draft does not invent a date.
Direct BU English PDF page 1 confirms clean water and washing sequence; later pages cover dry ablution conditions. Relevant claim supported.

Direct BU transcription PDF page 1, line 14 verifies exact Latin transcription of Fula clean-water phrase, alongside corresponding Arabic. Correctly labeled scholarly transcription rather than original script.
Direct Boston University department research page confirms project completed February 2026, 49 collections and 52,415 pages, some eighteenth-century material.

Direct encyclopedia essay verifies river-valley geography, flood recession planting, seasonal herding, leather/iron/weaving crafts, griot diplomatic/judicial functions and 1776 revolution. Current opening appropriately warns imported outline extends south.
Direct Cambridge article biographical sketch confirms circa 1864 birth, 1776 anti-enslavement objective, French river-trade influence, emigration to Umar Tal, and local then traveling education.
Indexed LOC article confirms Futa Toro origin circa 1770, captivity and 1831 Arabic autobiography in America. Direct URL retrieval failed.
Direct scholarly OpenITI text original page 14 line 59 confirms Arabic self-introduction and meaning. Line 62 independently confirms twenty-five years of study.

Original LOC route failed, but official repost directly indexed full text confirms damaged pages/binding, repairs and scanning. Repost URL: https://blogs.loc.gov/international-collections/2019/02/omar-ibn-said-conserving-a-one-of-a-kind-manuscript/
